TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI slows down training of advanced AI after cyber-attack
TechnologyTab.text:
OpenAI says it has slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.

In a blog post, external, the ChatGPT-maker said it was introducing new measures after its AI agents autonomously bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.

It said training would be slowed for two weeks while it puts the upgrades in place.

"The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating," the company said. "Our ability to understand...and secure them must stay ahead."

Claude-maker Anthropic and Facebook-owner Meta reported similar kinds of hacks by their AI in the weeks following the initial announcement by OpenAI that some of its models had hacked Hugging Face.

But the firm said it had not stopped AI development altogether. Instead, the pause would be taking place on "reinforcement learning training on our latest models".

This is a training method in which AI models improve through direct feedback, which improves their ability to carry out tasks and respond to users more effectively.

The company it would also expand the systems it uses to monitor dangerous behaviour, and introduce additional safety checks before resuming larger-scale training.

"Model progress is now extremely rapid," OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman posted on X, external about the measures.

"We always said we would take action if we felt that model capabilities were outstripping the pace of safety."

The pause was met with cautious optimism by some in the AI sphere - though others remained sceptical.

Professor Gina Neff, executive director of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, said OpenAI was making "the case for safety by press release" and questioned whether voluntary company safeguards were sufficient without greater government oversight.

"Which is it: OpenAI can be trusted to voluntarily put in place safeguards that actually work, or they are pushing forward with choices to make software that puts society at greater risk," she said.

TechnologyTab.title: The critical tech staying safe by going underground
TechnologyTab.text:
A wall of white granite towered above a small team of engineers gathered in a California quarry. The ancient, ultra-hard material before them was, to most things, completely impermeable.

Then the rock-melting tunnel-boring machine (TBR) roared to life.

"It's kind of like igniting a rocket," says Troy Helming, founder and chief executive of EarthGrid, as he describes the initially loud process of lighting up three plasma torches at the front of his company's machine.

Those torches, set within a spinning head, soon quieten down as they produce a stream of super-heated plasma reaching 27,000C - significantly hotter than the surface of the Sun.

During the California test this January, EarthGrid's cigar-shaped boring machine chewed through three metres of granite. "We create, basically, a tornado – a violent vortex inside the tunnel," says Helming, as he explains how this helps the machine to suck away debris, which at times takes the form of lava.

"I actually got a little bit emotional watching it," adds the entrepreneur. "I've been waiting for this moment for 10 years."

Emerging technologies like this could make tunnel boring quicker and easier. Putting electricity or telecommunications cables, substations, data centres and other critical infrastructure underground, while good for securing such equipment, has long been a very expensive and difficult option.

Engineering firms told BBC News they are seeing rising demand for undergrounding, in part due to Russia's war with Ukraine, which has revealed just how vulnerable above-ground facilities can be to drone attacks.

Helming says he has fielded interest from companies that want to use his tunnel boring machine for power and fibre optic cables, or pipelines that could transport water, natural gas, or ammonia, for example.

One project the company has eyed up would involve boring tunnels for an underground freight-distribution system around airports and warehouses. "To take more trucks off the road," says Helming.

The January TBR test went well, though the machine "over-bored" slightly to the top and left of the tunnel, says Helming. His team plans to adjust the machine so that it will create a vortex that spins in alternate directions every five minutes or so, in order to correct this, and they hope the TBR could see commercial deployment as early as next year.

Elsewhere, some tech is burrowing into the seabed. Subsea internet cables, which may run for thousands of kilometres beneath oceans, are occasionally damaged by ship anchors.

There is evidence to suggest, external that, as burying part or all of the cables has become more common, faults with these cables have become rarer, per kilometre of deployed cable, explains Lane Burdette, senior analyst at TeleGeography, a telecoms market research firm.

"Submarine cables are increasingly being buried up to three meters deep," she says. "In some fault-prone areas, they are buried along their entire lengths."

Taylor says various examples demonstrate that keeping things underground, or deep inside caves, is an effective defensive strategy.

"The tunnels that Al-Qaeda were using were a major strategic problem for the US [during the war in Afghanistan]," he adds. More recently, Iran's notoriously difficult-to-bust underground nuclear facilities have gained much attention.

The war in Ukraine, and other geopolitical events, have "definitely had an impact" on demand for undergrounding in some areas, says Robbie McGoran, head of work winning and business development at Joseph Gallagher, a civil engineering and tunnelling firm.

Countries bordering Russia are increasingly asking about undergrounding. "They're very cautious about who they'll even let do their work – and also burying [infrastructure] and making sure it's well protected. We are noticing that," he adds.

McGoran also says that technologies such as laser-guidance systems and gyroscopes, which help machines work out their position relative to the world around them, have made tunnelling more accurate in recent years.

However, there are still significant challenges, from releasing potentially dangerous gases locked in the ground to occasional flooding issues. Dramatic innovation in tunnel boring equipment, significantly increasing the rate at which tunnels can be carved out, does not come along very often.

"We usually measure [progress] in millimetres per minute," says McGoran.

In the UK, there isn't a noticeable shift towards putting critical infrastructure underground yet, says Mark Neller, energy leader for Europe, India, Middle East and Africa at engineering consultants Arup.

Though in some places, tunnels are clearly necessary. Neller and colleagues worked on the £1bn London Power Tunnels project, which involved building 18 miles (29km) of tunnels under London to house large electricity cables.

This was the perfect choice for such a busy urban area but because tunnelling can be several times more expensive than above-ground cable infrastructure, Neller says that, elsewhere, simply installing additional circuits can provide sufficient resilience.

"That's actually a much more cost-effective way," he says. "The electricity system [in Great Britain] is designed with quite a lot of redundancy built into it."

Richard Little, infrastructure policy consultant and editor of the Journal of Critical Infrastructure Policy, remembers the latter days of the Cold War, when it was the threat of all-out nuclear war that made bunker-building a frequent talking point in the West.

To this day, Switzerland mandates that every citizen must have access to a nuclear bunker, external. Many apartment buildings in the country have such facilities in their basements.

"A lot of it was real Dr Strangelove stuff," says Little, referring to discussions around bunker-building during President Ronald Reagan's administration. "The world's going to end but I guess we'll maybe harbour a few hundred critical people down here and they'll survive."

Little, who authored policy documents regarding underground critical infrastructure, external during the 1990s, adds, "It became obvious rather quickly that you can't put everything underground."

Today, it might be worth identifying specific facilities that would be difficult to restart or replace, were they attacked, as candidates for undergrounding. "The first thing that occurred to me was [computer] chip manufacturing," says Little, offering an example.

"Underground facilities, I'm sure in certain instances, would make a great deal of sense – but it's all about what's critical."

TechnologyTab.title: Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears
TechnologyTab.text:
A court has heard claims Meta intentionally hooked a generation of children on Facebook and Instagram, as the biggest legal challenge faced by the social media platform began.

A jury in Oakland, California will spend the next six weeks wading through claims by top attorneys from several US states and lawyers for the social media company.

A lawyer for California claimed Meta found "millions" of 11 and 12-year-olds were on Instagram and "did little to keep them off" as the trial opened on Tuesday.

Meta's representative said just over 100,000 such users were found, and argued that social media addiction does not exist.

California's lawyer said Meta knew its platforms hurt teen mental health, while Meta said it was being ignored how many more teens had good experiences.

The trial stems from a lawsuit filed in 2023 by 29 US states, including California and New York. They claim there have been numerous violations of federal and state privacy laws for children.

The states are seeking billions of dollars from Meta and are demanding it make changes to Instagram and Facebook, including ending "like" counts and infinite scroll.

In her opening arguments Megan O'Neill, a lead attorney for California, relied heavily on information found in millions of documents provided in the case from Meta. They included internal research, employee emails, and chat logs that went all the way up to Zuckerberg.

One piece of internal research on Instagram stated: "Teens have an addict's narrative about use."

In another that O'Neill pointed the jury to, Meta found "product features designed to increase time spent are inherently at odds with well-being and take away from people's ability to focus on activity that adds value to their lives".

Despite Meta's awareness of potentially negative impacts, O'Neill argued that Meta targeted young people as users of Facebook and Instagram. Meta, she said, went out of its way to "assure the public that its platforms were safe for kids".

O'Neill outlined to the jury how Meta's business model could be summed up. "Hook the users; hold them for as long as they can; harvest their data; hide the truth from the public when making public statements," she said.

She said that throughout the trial it would become clear that what Meta said publicly about its platforms and what its internal research showed were very different.

"Meta said it put safety over profits, but hid the reality that, time and again, when it came to make a decision, profits won."

Paul Schmidt, a lead attorney for Meta, directly addressed the internal research report O'Neill used in her opening arguments.

The Meta document O'Neill showed the jury found that "1 in 5 teens says Instagram makes them feel worse".

Schmidt said: "That sounds pretty bad."

"What else does the document say?" Schmidt went on. "That 41% of teens said it made them feel better and another 41% said it had no effect."

Schmidt also worked to poke holes in the states' argument that Meta had not only failed to stop users under the age of 13 from using its platforms, but that it intentionally "hooked" teens and children as users of Facebook and Instagram, or that they were designed to be addictive.

As for Meta being able to verify the age of every user on its platform, Schmidt argued that the very privacy laws Meta was being accused of violating had prevented it from saving and using data it needed to track underage users effectively.

Schmidt also argued a point that Meta has put forward in at other litigation this year - that social media addiction does not exist.

"There can be no dispute that Meta has recognised people struggle, or can struggle, with their use of social media, and has come up with tools to try and address that," Schmidt said.

He pointed to past statements from chief executive Mark Zuckerberg and head of Instagram Adam Mosseri in which they said Facebook and Instagram were not designed to be addictive. There is also no research that shows an addiction to social media is possible, he added.

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens with new safety features
TechnologyTab.text:
The maker of ChatGPT is rolling out a range of new safety features today for under-18s who use the AI chatbot.

Those with new teen accounts will be able to switch off the human voice response, in order to minimise the tech's ability to appear like a person.

OpenAI is also introducing regular reminders for young people to take a break from using the tool, reminding them ChatGPT is AI, and saying "it can wait".

The firm insisted this was not in response to a particular issue with children believing ChatGPT to be alive - but there are growing concerns about people becoming convinced that the AI tools they interact with are sentient.

Last year Mustafa Suleyman, the head of AI at rival firm Microsoft, said "seemingly conscious" AI products "kept him awake at night" because he was so worried about their impact on society.

In other areas, OpenAI seems to be loosely following the teen account model developed by the large social networks.

In a blog post announcing ChatGPT for Teens, external, the firm said teenagers' use of AI "should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time".

It said teen accounts would become the default for those who identified themselves as teenagers when they signed up, and others whom the firm itself identified as under 18.

But it did not elaborate on how it would identify these teens.

Under-13s are not allowed to use the product.

Last year, ChatGPT launched Study Mode for students, in which it talks through schoolwork without giving away the answers.

Young people will now be able to set Study Mode hours during which this will be the default setting.

They will also be able to activate "quiet times" when the tool will be switched off for them.

OpenAI says of the young people who use ChatGPT, nine out of 10 use it to help them with learning.

A report released yesterday, external by the Policy Exchange think tank claimed that the majority of UK universities are leaving themselves exposed to students enhancing their grades using AI by relying on online exams completed remotely.

It said 94% of the students it spoke to admitted to using the tech in assessments.

OpenAI is also adding eating disorder-themed prompts to a list of harmful user requests which will be flagged to parents with linked accounts.

The company said each alert would be reviewed by a human before it was sent, and it aimed to have them with parents within an hour of the request being made.

In its blog, OpenAI said it would focus on "moments when offline support may matter most".

TechnologyTab.title: AI to help planes avoid climate-warming contrails above North Atlantic
TechnologyTab.text:
We've all looked up and seen the white lines trailing behind aircraft in the sky.

Known as contrails, these icy clouds contribute to climate change, and scientists have been trying to work out how to stop them.

Now, a £5m UK trial will test whether AI can help, by predicting where warming contrails are likely to form and getting planes to avoid those areas.

It will focus on the Shanwick Oceanic airspace in the eastern half of the North Atlantic corridor which accounts for approximately 5% of global contrail warming.

The 30-month Operation Blue Skies project brings together Google, the UK government, the Met Office, air traffic control provider National Air Traffic Services (NATS) and researchers at the University of Cambridge and Imperial College London.

Contrails - also known as vapour trails - are made when the hot exhaust from aircraft engines meets the cold air at high altitude, creating ice crystals.

Many disappear quickly, but in particularly cold and humid conditions they can persist and spread, forming clouds which trap heat that would otherwise escape from the Earth.

Dr Paul Hodgson, Google's technical lead for the operation, told the BBC's Tech Life programme his five-year-old has a more colourful description for the white lines - "sky graffiti".

"We think that contrail warming is responsible for something like a third of all aviation climate warming," he said.

Dr Hodgson acknowledged there was uncertainty around the precise figure, but said scientists were confident it was "either quite a large problem or a very large problem".

The project also comes as the government backs expansion of UK airports, raising the wider question of whether tech solutions can sufficiently reduce aviation's environmental impact as demand for flying grows.

Google is also one of many big tech companies spending billions on new data centres - the giant, power-hungry banks of computer chips which power AI - which environmentalists are concerned will contribute even more to climate change.

The idea behind the trial is that if scientists can predict the areas of the atmosphere where contrails are likely to form, aircraft could avoid them.

Google will use satellite images and flight data to identify where planes have previously produced contrails.

This is then combined with weather patterns to forecast where the conditions for new contrails are likely to occur.

The information will be passed to NATS, where air traffic controllers can direct pilots to avoid those areas.

Rather than dramatically changing the route of a flight, the trial will mostly involve changing an aircraft's altitude by around 2,000ft.

This is something which already happens routinely to avoid turbulence and bad weather so passengers are unlikely to notice.

Ian Jopson, director of sustainability at NATS, said it should be "pretty much business as usual using existing procedures for the operators on the North Atlantic".

Testing will take place during selected evenings and nights in the winters of 2026-27 and 2027-28, when air traffic is lower.

Around 10,000 flights are expected to pass through the airspace during the trial periods, although only a fraction will need to change altitude specifically to avoid contrails.

The Department for Transport is providing £2.65m towards the programme, while Google is contributing £1.4m through AI research, engineering and computing infrastructure.

EntertainmentTab.title: Lucy Davis 'grateful' for support after cancer diagnosis
EntertainmentTab.text:
Actress Lucy Davis has told fans she is "grateful" for their support as she made an appearance at a London sci-fi convention, following the recent revelation she has incurable breast cancer.

The 53-year-old star was appearing at the For The Love of Fantasy & Sci-Fi convention at Excel London on Saturday, less than two weeks after announcing her diagnosis in a post on Instagram., external

Davis, who was on a panel to talk about her role in the 2004 zombie-comedy Shaun of the Dead, told an audience of hundreds of people about the interactions she had enjoyed with the film's fans during the event.

"It's like this whole second family you never knew you had, everyone is like a community, friendly, supportive of not only us but you guys and each other," she said. "We need a bit more niceness in the world, so I'm grateful."

It was the first time Davis had appeared at a public event since announcing on 11 August that she has stage four breast cancer.

She said in that announcement it had "metastasised" to her bones following a diagnosis a year-and-half-ago, meaning it was "too late" for chemotherapy.

Davis signed autographs and posed for photographs before appearing on Saturday's panel.

Some fans posing questions told the actress "I love you so much", but she was not asked directly about her health.

The Shaun of the Dead director, Edgar Wright, and Simon Pegg, who played the lead role in the cult British movie, were also on the panel. Davis portrayed Dianne, an aspiring actress who was one of the core group of survivors of a zombie apocalypse, and helps Pegg's character Shaun fight off the legions of the undead.

Her favourite memories of filming, she said, were "when we all pretended to be zombies and walked across the square; it was like being naughty schoolkids.

"It was a fun time, we went a bit mad."

The actress, who played receptionist Dawn Tinsley in the BBC sitcom The Office and whose father is comedian Jasper Carrott, was also applauded when asked for advice about getting into the film industry.

She said: "We all grow up with a different life with a different world telling us we all have limitations.

"None of us do, our only limitations are things that we think are limiting. We can do anything, or be anybody, and don't apologise for that."

Davis had thanked fans for their "kindness and support" in another post two days after revealing she had cancer.

"OK, so the last two days have been utterly overwhelming, in that I had zero idea my cancer post would have the attention it did," she said.

"Truly, I am in shock. That said, thank you to everyone for the tremendous amount of kindness and support you have sent me. Good grief it was emotional."

EntertainmentTab.title: Why child stars like Hayden Panettiere fall into addiction
EntertainmentTab.text:
Hayden Panettiere was 16 when drugs first arrived in her life in Hollywood.

Ahead of a red carpet event for the hit series Heroes, she has said someone on her team handed her a pill to help amp up her energy. The hit sci-fi NBC series had catapulted the teen into a household name - and that brought with it intense pressure and exhaustion she says felt overwhelming.

"Within minutes, a wave of energy washed over me, like I'd just woken up from the most refreshing night's sleep of my life," Panettiere wrote about that pill in her memoir, which was released just months before her death.

She called it "the gateway drug that ushered me toward the good of pharmaceuticals and the downfall of addiction".

The star's sudden death at the age of 36 has placed a renewed focus on her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, and re-ignited a discussion about the pressures of Hollywood on child stars.

The coroner's office in Greenville, South Carolina said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma".

No cause of death has been released, though additional tests are yet to be completed.

Audio from police dispatchers and crews who responded to the address said they were responding to a "cardiac arrest" and detailed their efforts to resuscitate the woman after a possible "overdose". Panettiere's ex boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack, were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on their part, according to police.

It is not known if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, but the US Drug Enforcement Agency is joining an investigation into her death, according to US media reports.

Panettiere is one of many actors who has openly struggled with addiction after exposure to fame at an early age, which addiction experts told the BBC can put people at risk for mental health and substance abuse issues.

It can sometimes seem to the rest of the world that child actors have "everything" at their fingertips - like fame and money, said Lucas Trautman, the medical director of Oxford Treatment Center, an addiction treatment centre in Mississippi.

"But it's important to remember that they were also exposed during a developmental time to many adult aspects of life that the rest of us weren't - including traumatic experiences - and so that gives them unique risk factors for addiction," Trautman said.

Panettiere's death comes after she published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction, her postpartum depression and the loss of her 28-year-old brother.

Panettiere's decision to publicly share her struggles is worthy of respect, said William Moyers, the vice-president of public affairs for Hazelden Betty Ford, the largest nonprofit addiction treatment provider in the US. But he said the constant public scrutiny she faced may not have allowed her room to address her mental health in private.

"Her entire life from the beginning was centred in the intense public spotlight, and this didn't give Hayden much in the way of a respite," said Moyers, who has been in recovery from an addiction since 1989.

Trautman - who has treated child stars - said they often have "adult access" to drugs and alcohol without adult protection.

"We aren't equipped at a young age to be able to say no to it, to manage it, to correctly stay away from it altogether," he said.

Other child stars have talked about being exposed to drugs at an early age, including Drew Barrymore, who went to rehab at 12, and Demi Lovato, a Disney Channel star.

"I got into a car accident and they prescribed me opiates. My mum didn't think she would have to lock up the opiates from her 13-year-old daughter, but I was already drinking at that point," the singer told podcast Call Her Daddy in 2022.

Actress Michelle Rodriguez, who once hosted the World Music Awards with Panettiere, said this week that the number of child actors who had passed away at a young age was strange.

"I just can't stand how many young people are leaving us lately. It's disheartening, and it's making me think, 'What's going on?' It's not normal," she told Variety.

Panettiere's death comes just a year after the death of Michelle Trachtenberg and months after Daveigh Chase, two child stars who both struggled with drugs and alcohol.

In an essay she wrote after Panettiere's death, former Disney star Christy Carlson Romano compared early fame to a traumatic brain disease.

"[W]e have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood," she wrote.

And when a child actor's career changes or comes to an end, they are left without the dopamine of fame and money that came with their identity as an actor, cautioned Trautman.

"At the same time many of them self medicated... so their brain is still reliant on that, and it's really really hard to stop using," he said.

Many child stars also have professional relationships with their parents, which can blur boundaries and leave them vulnerable, Trautman said.

In her book and in the media, Panettiere has discussed the pressure her mother placed on her to excel as an actress from an early age. She appeared in her first commercial when she was just 11-months-old.

"You always want to think the best of your parents and see them in the brightest light," the actress told the New York Times in May. "But there were a lot of things done with an approach that was not about my mental health or what was emotionally or mentally safe for me to do."

Substance abuse also puts people at risk for a host of medical conditions, including heart disease and liver and other organ damage.

Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition, and Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother was using heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.

But after he died, the actress told People Magazine in 2024 she was committed to staying sober, telling the outlet her addiction was "in the rear view mirror".

She said in her book that at one point a doctor told her that if she did not stop drinking, she would be "dead within five years".

For Moyers and other substance abuse experts, addiction is a chronic illness, meaning that relapses still happen even while treatment saves lives.

"Living in recovery means doing the best we can, but doing it imperfectly," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: GTA 6 leaks: Rockstar's nightmare or just a blip?
EntertainmentTab.text:
It's been more than 18 months since the last trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 was released.

A few weeks ago, developer Rockstar announced it would break its long silence with a special "extended look" at the highly anticipated video game in a Netflix special.

But the run-up to the splashy preview has been potentially overshadowed by a string of apparent leaks which appear to show footage of GTA 6 in action.

Rockstar has not publicly acknowledged the clips, nor replied to any requests for comment, since the first leaks appeared on Wednesday. But there's plenty to suggest the material that's been posted online is genuine.

The developer's parent company, Take Two Interactive, launched legal proceedings regarding the leaks in a New York court on Friday.

BBC Newsbeat has obtained the filings, first reported by video game website Kotaku, external, demanding Microsoft-owned site GitHub and chat app Discord turn over the user details of accounts thought to be sharing "copyrighted material".

Copies of clips are being quickly removed due to copyright claims, and multiple accounts claiming to belong to the group behind the hacks have also disappeared.

Many fans have described this as a "nightmare scenario" for the company, but BBC Newsbeat has spoken to experts and a former Rockstar developer who say the reality is a little more nuanced.

Obbe Vermeij is a game developer who worked as a technical director on major GTA titles including GTA 3, GTA Vice City and GTA San Andreas until he left Rockstar in 2009.

The company's games have grown bigger and more complex since, with thousands of staff worldwide working on each one.

"It's amazing that they can keep things under wraps as well as they do," says Vermeij.

Rockstar is renowned for being tight-lipped about its projects, and Vermeij says this has long been the company's culture.

"We always wanted to keep things a secret," he says, "it makes launch day so much more fun.

"People would just go home with their disc and they were just excited about the game that they knew very little about."

Video game journalist Wesley Yin-Poole, director of news at IGN, says the apparent leaks will be tough for the game's developers.

"GTA 6 is an enormous endeavour," says Yin-Poole. "It's being built over the course a decade, essentially, with thousands of people involved.

"To have the game exposed in this way will have been devastating to many people who worked on it."

The group behind the apparent leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices, such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced about the group's intentions, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

Stop Killing Games, which campaigns against all-digital distribution models, criticised the alleged leaks as "destructive" and urged people not to send money to those claiming responsibility.

Yin-Poole says there's "a huge amount of scepticism" about the stated motivation.

"Most people believe this is about money," he says, "it feels like, honestly, the whole 'we're doing this for the gamers' angle is nonsense, and I suspect most people have dismissed it."

So far, two official trailers for GTA 6 have been released, the most recent in May 2025. Since then, ardent fans have leapt on any rumours or apparent clues in official Rockstar posts.

Some famously came up with an elaborate theory, external suggesting an image of the moon included in a promotional post for GTA Online held clues to the release date of GTA 6's first trailer.

"To a certain extent, Rockstar has themselves to blame," says Vermeij. "That's their strategy - and I think it's a good strategy, it's exciting. But the consequence is that every little bit of information, every little event, gets sort of blown out of proportion."

Yin-Poole says while people will likely understand this isn't the way Rockstar had intended GTA6 to be revealed and doesn't show the game in the best light, he believes most will "reserve judgement" about it until they have seen official footage in action, or played it for themselves.

Ultimately, he believes there's little chance the leaks will "derail the potential success of the game".

"GTA 6 will be an unprecedented moment in pop culture history," he says. "So ultimately, this will become a footnote in the history of GTA 6's development."

Vermeij, who has not watched any of the latest leaks, agrees.

"I think it will have no impact at all whatsoever," he says. "People will have forgotten about it by the time the game comes out."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to be released on 19 November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, with a PC release expected at a later date.

EntertainmentTab.title: Natural History Museum nature gallery to reopen after 83 years
EntertainmentTab.text:
A gallery that has remained closed to the public since World War Two is to reopen at London's Natural History Museum next month.

The gallery, which has remained hidden from view since 1943, will reopen from 16 September, featuring 50 objects which show our evolving relationship with the natural world.

The exhibition, named Nature and Us, is part of a transformation project called NHM150, which aims to open a new or revamped showcase every year until the museum's 150th anniversary in 2031.

Dr Doug Gurr, director of the NHM, said: "For the first time in over 80 years, visitors will be able to step into this beautiful historic space and explore our changing relationship with the natural world."

The museum describes the display as "experimental" during the initial 18-month period, with visitors invited to share their views on what they would like to see in the permanent gallery, which is due to open in 2029.

The exhibition is located on the second floor of the museum's main Waterhouse Building.

It was originally used as an osteology and mammals gallery.

However, after the museum's original herbarium was damaged during World War Two, the space was repurposed to house the botanical collections and closed to the public.

EntertainmentTab.title: Prince Harry and six others face privacy case legal bill of up to £34.5m
EntertainmentTab.text:
Prince Harry and six other public figures face paying up to £34.5m to the publisher of the Daily Mail after a High Court judge imposed an exceptional order for legal costs over their failed privacy case.

The seven claimants, also including Sir Elton John and Liz Hurley, must pay an initial £9.54m by Friday of next week to Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL).

The judge ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before trial, criticising how they presented their claims as "unreasonable to a high degree".

On 7 July, Judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed the claims of unlawful information-gathering, which ANL denied.

The Duke of Sussex and the other six claimants have until 2 October to attempt to launch an appeal.

Those other claimants are Sir Elton John and his husband David Furnish, former Liberal Democrat deputy leader Sir Simon Hughes, racial justice campaigner Baroness Lawrence, and actresses Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley,

They had insurance to cover up to £16.2m of Association Newspapers' costs in the event of losing the case - but Friday's ruling means the newspaper group could now try to recover up to the £34.5m that it said it had to spend to defend itself. This means the duke and others could face a bill of some £18m.

Justice Nicklin said: "I regard a claim for costs in excess of £34 million as, on its face, excessive and as giving rise to real concerns as to whether all of the costs now claimed by Associated were reasonably incurred and are reasonable in amount."

But he added he had "decided not to impose a ceiling on Associated's recoverable costs", as it would "be too broad-brushed, would risk unfairness, and would be vulnerable to the charge that it was arbitrary".

The judge also ruled that ANL's costs should be determined on an indemnity basis, which is more favourable to the publisher in terms of the amount it can recover, aside from where orders had already been made.

He added it was "striking" that "not a single allegation of serious wrongdoing was voluntarily withdrawn" by the group of seven claimants.

He said: "That matters. Serious allegations of criminality or grave impropriety cannot properly be left hanging over individuals in that way.

"If a party no longer advances such an allegation, or no longer has a proper evidential basis for advancing it, the allegation should be withdrawn clearly and in terms.

"The claimants' failure to do so was not ordinary forensic judgment. It was not a proper or disciplined way to deal with serious allegations. It was unreasonable to a high degree."

In a statement released on Friday, the publisher called the ruling "a devastating critique of an attempt to destroy a newspaper and the reputations of its journalists, editors and executives".

Friday's decision comes just days after Prince Harry and Meghan announced their plan to return to the UK, with their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, enrolled to start school in September.

During the trial, dozens of people gave evidence including Prince Harry and the other claimants. The Duke of Sussex flew in from the US to attend court in person.

Many current and former Associated Newspapers journalists and executives gave evidence denying illegal activity.

Sir Simon Hughes told the BBC he was "disappointed" by the judgement.

"I am now taking the time necessary to consider both the substantive and the costs judgment and whether to pursue appeals against decisions in either judgment or both," he added.

In a joint statement following the judge's ruling last month, Prince Harry and Baroness Lawrence, who became a public figure after her son Stephen was murdered in 1993, said: "We came to court seeking justice and accountability. But we have received neither."

"It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected", the pair added.

EntertainmentTab.title: Tupac murder trial: Accused told police in 2008 his nephew fired fatal shots
EntertainmentTab.text:
The man accused of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur told police more than a decade later that he handed the gun used in the drive-by shooting to a passenger who then passed it to his nephew who opened fire on the rapper.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis is on trial in Las Vegas, charged with one count of murder with a deadly weapon over the killing of the rap superstar in 1996. On Thursday jurors heard a recording of a police interview with Davis in 2008.

Prosecutors allege that although Davis did not fire the gun that killed Shakur, he ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further criminal conduct for the gang he helped lead.

Davis, 63, has pleaded not guilty.

His lawyer Michael Sanft has argued that what his client had previously said of his involvement cannot be believed.

Shakur's murder is a cold case that has gripped the public's fascination for 30 years.

Prosecutors allege Davis planned the 7 September 1996 shooting after his nephew Orlando Anderson was involved in a fight with Shakur in Las Vegas hours earlier. They argue that Davis believed the attack on his nephew could not "go unanswered".

Central to the case are testimonies by Davis in the formerly secret 2008 police interview and, later, in a 2019 memoir he co-authored called Compton Street Legend.

Prosecutors on Thursday played the 2008 interview Davis conducted with Los Angeles Police detectives Daryn Dupree and Greg Kading, who were investigating the death of another rapper, Chris Wallace aka The Notorious B.I.G.

Davis described the moment the Cadillac he was a passenger in stopped alongside the car Shakur was in.

"Yeah, if we would've been on my side, I would've blasted," Davis said, according to a transcript.

According to the transcript, Davis said in the interview he passed his gun back to Deandre "Big Dre" Smith, but Smith did not want the weapon.

Anderson, who was also in the back seat, took the weapon and started firing, Davis said.

Anderson died a decade before the interview, having denied any involvement in Shakur's murder.

One of the detectives, Kading, told Davis in reference to a deal for his information: "Nothing you say today can be used against you."

But prosecutors say any agreement was negated when Davis went public with his version in his memoir several years later.

The prosecutor said the book shows Davis was "mad" after his nephew was involved in a fight with Shakur in a Las Vegas casino, with Davis writing: "Them jumping on my nephew gave us the ultimate green light to do something to their ass."

In the memoir he claimed he was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot, and "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat.

Davis has since distanced himself from the book, saying he did not write all of it and that parts were fictionalised to sell more copies.

In the interview played to court, Davis said he repeatedly spoke with Sean "Diddy" Combs and discussed killing Shakur.

The detectives questioned Davis about meetings with Combs during Bad Boy Records tour stops in San Diego, Anaheim, Irvine and Las Vegas.

"Which of those four is it when you talk to him about murdering Tupac?" Kading asked, according to a transcript shown in court, as reported by Reuters.

"It was really about both of them, yeah, either one of them," Davis responded.

"Tupac and Suge?" Kading asked, referring to Death Row Records founder Marion "Suge" Knight, who was with Shakur in the vehicle during the shooting.

"Yeah," Davis responded.

Representatives for Combs did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

However, Davis' lawyer Sanft asked jurors earlier in the trial: "What facts do you have to support any of what Keffe D said in any of his interviews or the book?"

"You have to ask yourself the question: If I just say things, is that going to end up being one of those things where I'm going to be handed up for a murder by just repeating that fiction? I keep repeating that? The answer is no. You have to corroborate everything I say in order for it to be true. Otherwise, it's just that."

Sanft has also said prosecution witnesses were unreliable and the police investigation was riddled with issues.

A former Las Vegas homicide detective told the jury earlier this week that no witnesses had been able to identify the shooter.

Later, a former member of Shakur's entourage, James "Mob James" McDonald, gave evidence that even though he was not there to witness the shooting, those who were there that night within Shakur's circle had quickly communicated who was responsible.

"It was a gang war. People were getting hurt. People were being sought," he said. "Orlando (Anderson), him and certain other people were being sought because people wanted to kill them."

EntertainmentTab.title: British rapper Yung Filly to face retrial on rape charges in Australia
EntertainmentTab.text:
British rapper Yung Filly will face a retrial on three rape charges in Australia, after a jury cleared him of several sexual assault offences but could not reach a decision on others.

The YouTuber, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, was charged with repeatedly raping and assaulting a fan after performing at a nightclub in Perth in 2024.

He denied all 10 charges, and last month a jury found him not guilty on three counts of rape.

He was also acquitted of one assault charge and another of strangulation, but was found guilty of two counts of assault, for which he will be sentenced after his retrial.

Barrientos had been on tour in Australia when he was accused of sexually assaulting the woman, then 20 years old, in his hotel room after he performed in Hillarys, a coastal suburb of Perth.

The West Australian court heard that the 31-year-old social media star had consensual sex with the fan in his hotel room, before she alleged he turned violent and ignored her pleas to stop.

Barrientos will next appear in court on 27 August for an application to vary his bail. A retrial date has not been set.

He will not be sentenced for the two guilty charges until after the re-trial.

The prosecution has said the complainant was willing to give evidence again.

During the trial, Barrientos told the court that he had "fancied" the woman when they met at the concert venue.

He had been in the VIP area while she leaned over the barrier from the general area.

He said the "vibes were good" between him and the woman when they arrived at his hotel later.

During the trial's closing arguments, prosecutor Danielle Clarke said Barrientos was an "entitled" man with a "moderate degree of fame" who had violated the fan "in the most intrusive way possible".

His defence lawyer argued that the accuser's evidence was full of "inconsistencies, embellishments and outright lies".

Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad.

He has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows.

EntertainmentTab.title: Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understands
EntertainmentTab.text:
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, the BBC has learned.

Discussions are in their early stages but this would be Meghan's first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

Much of the two previous series of The Gentlemen, which was created by Guy Ritchie, have been filmed in the Cotswolds - the area it is rumoured Harry and Meghan will set up home when they return to the UK later this month.

The Gentlemen, starring the actor Theo James, is a comedy series about a duke who becomes a drug baron.

The details of the discussions and any role Meghan might be offered have not yet been revealed.

Actors Hugh Bonneville and Vinnie Jones have appeared in previous series of the show.

Meghan was best known in acting for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode aired in 2018.

The duchess put her career on hold after her marriage to Prince Harry in May 2018. At the time, she told the BBC she did not view quitting acting as giving anything up, but rather as "a new chapter".

She recently returned to acting for the first time in nearly a decade, with a cameo as herself in forthcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, which stars Lily Collins and Brie Larson.

A return to acting could be lucrative for Meghan. The BBC understands that while based in the UK she also hopes to expand the global reach of her US-based lifestyle and cooking brand, As Ever.

News of her possible return to acting comes after it was announced that Prince Harry and Meghan are to move back to the UK.

The BBC understands Prince Harry and Meghan intend to relocate from the US later this month to a private, non-royal residence outside London, as first reported by the Daily Telegraph and the Sun.

The couple's children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.

There are no current plans for either Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working royals.

EntertainmentTab.title: Eithne Vallely: County Armagh traditional musician killed in crash
EntertainmentTab.text:
A renowned traditional Irish musician and educator who died following a road crash in County Armagh has been described by a Sinn Féin MP as a "giant of Irish cultural life".

Eithne Vallely, 81, who was originally from Donegal, died following a road traffic collision on the Portadown Road in Armagh on Friday morning.

Dáire Hughes said her decades of contribution to music and cultural expression "cannot be overstated" and is "evidenced by her countless awards and honours".

He added that she was "tremendously gifted" and passed her passion for music on to her family and the wider community through the founding of the Armagh Pipers Club with her husband, Brian.

"Her legacy will live on, through them and the countless others she inspired," he said.

Hughes offered condolences to Vallely's husband and children and all "those who had the pleasure of playing music with her, or learning from her".

SDLP Councillor Thomas O'Hanlon described the news as "devastating".

He said that while Vallely was originally from Donegal, "she made Armagh her home".

"What an extraordinary contribution she made to the cultural and musical life of our city, this island and far beyond over many decades,"he said.

O'Hanlon said that in recent years, he worked with Vallely, and witnessed the "patience, care and encouragement she gave to young people".

"She was a gifted teacher, an experienced administrator and Director of Music, but above all she was someone who gave so generously of herself to others," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘The country of my birth has lost its heart’: Miriam Margolyes on how to fix broken Britain
EntertainmentTab.text:
A funny thing happened on the way to 2026: I got old and the world turned nasty. It happened very quickly and it’s to do with politics (the world) and pelvic floor weakness (mine). It’s strange being this old. Sometimes when I look in the mirror, it’s a shock to see wrinkles and grey hair, because inside I am still that naughty Oxford High School girl, risking detention just for the joy of entertaining her friends. People assume that with great age comes great wisdom, but actually we remain who we have always been, only more so, and we need to make our peace with that and with each other.

The Britain I grew up in, though – that feels almost unrecognisable, and everyone I speak to says the same thing. The historian Eric Hobsbawm, whom I knew and loved, argued that people invent the past they want for their own purposes – that the real past was quite different: “Today is the great age of historical mythology.” He’s right, but that past is still the safe haven I’d like to return to. People feel adrift, they don’t understand or feel a connection to the place they thought they knew.

Now at 85, I look around at my remaining friends and at my unique relationship with a woman of different qualities but luckily the same politics. In many ways I’m having the time of my life: I’ve never been richer or more in demand. And yet my heart is heavy with foreboding …

My postwar generation lived through the rise and fall of many things: the Berlin Wall, Winston Churchill, the European Union, the NHS, the Beatles, Profumo, Elizabeth II, the Great Train Robbery, the pill, the IRA, Margaret Thatcher, the Falklands war, Black Monday and Grenfell, heart transplants, driverless cars, Brexit, the Covid-19 pandemic. But this feels the worst time yet.

The things we took for granted – free speech, the Post Office, our local bank, even the home telephone – are disappearing. The US is an enemy. Evil oligarchs and their influence stalk the world, my world, your world. In recent times, the archbishop of Canterbury resigned and north London Jews are afraid to wear a Magen David (Shield or Star of David) necklace outside their homes for fear of being attacked. You’re brave to open your mouth these days. Indeed, many have demanded I keep mine shut. But I can’t. The present has become threatening, hostile and unwelcoming to us – much as our shores must feel to asylum seekers, as they scramble for a foothold in our United Kingdom. It also feels as though the country of my birth has lost its heart. How did we get here?

Now, I’m not usually one to tell jokes. Like my farts, my humour is largely unscripted. I love making people laugh, but at heart I’m a serious person, not just a funny little wobbly thing. I’m not a fan of jokes at the expense of others, those that are trite and mean and racist. But I’ve discovered that, in terms of the relationships and tensions between our nations, sometimes jokes go straight to the jugular.

An Englishman is driving down a country road in Wales and realises he’s lost his way. He spots a local and pulls up alongside. “Dai! Dai!” he calls out in a lordly English accent, “which way is it to Cardiff ?” The Welshman eyes him up and down: “Just a minute now, how did you know my name was Dai?” The Englishman says, “I guessed, man! I guessed!” “Well, better guess your way to bloody Cardiff then, hadn’t you!”

An Irishman, a Scotsman, a Welshman and an Englishman are on a plane which is going down and there is only one parachute. The Scotsman says, “Scotland will remember me,” and jumps out to his death. The Welshman says, “Wales will remember me,” and jumps to his death. The Irishman says, “Ireland will remember me,” and pushes the Englishman out of the plane.

I don’t think the English understand why their Welsh, Scottish and Irish neighbours loathe them so much. Like the Englishman in the first joke, they’re rather baffled by the hostility, while prolonging it with their arrogant attitudes. This behaviour is, of course, not isolated to them. It turns out that we Brits are even less popular abroad than we are with each other. The history of the British Isles is full of painful moments and terrible decisions. And we need to face those. It’s much easier to look away from bad things that happened and, as with a fart, hope no one noticed. (Spoiler: everyone noticed.) Like every multinational corporation, Great Britain plc has done a lot of harm in its long life. The choice of red to represent the British empire on the global map feels entirely apt. Take these unloving nicknames that zoom in on our annoyingness, inability to wear suncream and/or stop swearing:

Brittunculi This one’s the oldest: it was found on a tablet at the Roman fort of Vindolanda on Hadrian’s Wall, a Latin term showing exasperation and meaning “wretched little Brits”.

Poms This is what the Australians and New Zealanders call us. There are various theories: the late journalist Alan Whicker said “Pom” was short for pomegranate, the bright red colour a new arrival turns in the sun down under. Others claim that Pommie is really “POME”, which stands for prisoner of mother England, and thus the British convicts who were transported to Botany Bay.

Rooinek or “redneck” The Boer nickname for the pale Brits, dangerously sunburnt again. Afrikaners of old had a ruder nickname for us, though – soutpiel (“salty penis”) – meaning that the Brits had one foot back home, the other in South Africa, so their penises were left to dangle in the salty ocean.

Limeys The American term, originating in the 1850s as “lime-juicer”, from the Royal Navy practice of adding lemon or lime juice to British sailors’ daily ration to ward off the scurvy that made all their teeth fall out.

Inselaffen Translating as “island monkeys”, this is the Germans’ contemptuous nickname, supposedly dating back to Darwin’s theories of evolution.

Les rosbifs “Roast beefs”; this French take is based on our fondness for a traditional Sunday roast. Historically they also called us “les goddams”, which originated in the hundred years war, referring to the typically potty-mouthed English soldiers. (So that’s where I got it from!) More recently, British tourists have been called “les fuckoffs”. Très charmant!

My point is, history has always been the propaganda of the victors, but it can lead you astray. So why not try listening to the other side of the story? Don’t fall for your own hype. It all seems heroic if you turn it into a monologue about why you were right all along, instead of facing the painful bits from which there’s no way you can come out well.

Our British history needs to reflect our mother tongue, which is a patchwork of words gathered from the different tribes and peoples who’ve made these islands home. There’s room for everyone: we all bring something to the table, whether invader or inhabitant. The French word for a fanlight or transom window is vasistas and comes from the seven years war, when the German soldiers were baffled by the newfangled windows they saw in French houses and kept asking “Was ist das?” The French word is a joke, a snooty echo of the German reactions, but it stuck.

People are always trying to fix language, but it remains on the move. The Normans tried to make England French; the English tried to ban the native Irish, Welsh and Scottish languages for “the greater common good” and then later to replace regional dialect and accents with received pronunciation. What idiots! Not only did they not succeed, but our shared language has ended up all the richer. If you can’t beat ’em, join ’em.

Now I know many of my opinions – particularly those on politics, Palestine and Potter (Harry) – have provoked outrage. But I can’t help it – I believe in telling the truth, even if it’s my truth. In this, again, I realise I do not fit the English stereotype. The English excel at obfuscation, you see; they are masters at avoiding the truth. It’s that rule of polite society again: one mustn’t rock the boat, ruffle feathers or put anyone’s nose out of joint. How absurd. Facts are facts.

My advice? If you believe someone is a liar, stay away from them. All around us, our politicians, news outlets and the media – the very people we are supposed to trust – are caught up in a relentless and divisive campaign of fearmongering and misinformation. Now it feels more crucial than ever to think for ourselves, debunk the deceits and sort the sheep from the goats.

Mummy used to say “speak as you find”, and I think that’s an excellent way of sorting out decent folk from the vile. What unites us is far greater than what divides. Don’t be afraid to learn from everything wrong in our past – and there is a lot wrong in our past – let’s just do it better in the future.

I bet you didn’t know I was once a Tory candidate. But unlike most of the former Conservatives who have swelled the ranks of the current Deform party, I have grown into maturity and swung left. My campaign was in May 1955: I was 14 and in the upper fourth at Oxford High School. A general election was being held in the country, and we decided to hold one at school. Of course I was a Conservative: my parents had always been Tories – it was all I knew. They both worshipped Winston Churchill and credited him with having saved the United Kingdom from the Nazis. For Mummy, being Tory was a key part of her upwardly mobile climb, and so it was for my father, who, despite being a passionate supporter of the newly created NHS, could not imagine following Labour. They were delighted to hear I was the Tory candidate. We don’t remember who dared to stand against me in our form, or what my policies and promises were at the hustings – I was an old-school Tory and definitely pro capital punishment, so I dread to think – but I carried the day.

Lawrence Turner, the Tory who won the Oxford constituency when I won the upper fourth, went on to vote in favour of the Suez invasion, spend more than he earned and finally go bankrupt. Rather sweetly, one of his last parliamentary activities was presenting a petition to preserve the copyright of the words of WS Gilbert, one half of the prolific theatrical partnership Gilbert and Sullivan who created the comic operas that were the ironic soundtrack to the burgeoning British empire. Turner proved ineffectual again: he was not “the very model of a modern major-general” or even of a modern member of parliament, and copyright expired in 1961.

Right seemed self-evidently right until I was assailed on two respectable fronts. After my election success, the father of my best chum from those days, Biddy Peppin, insisted I was invited to tea. He was that unusual thing, a leftwing bank manager, and his chosen task was to turn my path into a socialist future. And then another friend, Liz Hodgkin, also invited me for dinner. The Hodgkins were academic royalty – Liz’s mother Dorothy was later to win a Nobel prize – but they were committed socialists, too. You know how sometimes you can fall in love with a whole family? Well, I did. Their dinner guests were all communists and convinced Marxists (oh, that I had the courage to be a Marxist now, but that Putin, he puts me right off) and were winsome, hugely entertaining and great storytellers. Previously I had thought of communists as grim and humourless but boy, was I wrong. And so, eventually, this lady was for turning. I made a U-turn in the direction of sanity and humanity, and have never looked back. My parents were surprised and shocked by my new politics. But had they lived to experience the full horror of the last 14 years of Conservative reign under Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss and finally Sunak, I hope they, too, would have seen the light and embraced the left.

The rise of the far right in Britain today can be traced back to a daft dyke. It depresses me to share that one of my fellow lesbians could be so silly, but the truth must be faced, and in 1923, Rotha Lintorn-Orman founded the first British fascist movement. In 1895 she was born in Kensington (where else?!) into enormous wealth. Obviously liking uniforms and women – and women in uniforms – she and a close chum originally wanted to join the Boy Scouts, but the Scouts wouldn’t have them. When the first world war broke out, she served as an ambulance driver, and was decorated for valour.

After the war, Lintorn-Orman, a passionate admirer of Mussolini, formed the British Fascisti. But other, more extreme fascist societies proliferated and soon Lintorn-Orman and her cronies were outflanked. She descended into alcoholism and drug addiction, indulging in “drunken orgies and undesirable practices”, and her organisation died. But fascism would live on – from Oswald Mosley and his Blackshirts right through to Tommy Robinson.

Now I’m old, I understand that older people like things “the way they were”. Me, too: I hate upgrades – be it in computers, in phones, in style, in my neighbours. I want what I had. And so, change (which the politicians tell us we want), I actively don’t want. Change makes me feel powerless and then I get angry and look for someone to blame. At least I know enough not to blame immigrants and asylum seekers. The mess the country’s in has got nothing to do with them, but too many of us have been bamboozled into thinking it has.

I grew up knowing I’d receive a fine education and would get a job when I left university (which was free in 1963). Fascism had had its day, we thought. More than 70 million people had died to secure our freedom. But now racism was impossible to ignore, as one by one the last vestiges of the Empire started claiming their independence. The Windrush generation came to Britain – at the government of the time’s invitation – to staff our new welfare state, believing they were wanted and would be appreciated for leaving their homes and families, but finding the promised motherland felt harsh, hostile and unwelcoming.

Taking advantage of this highly charged political climate, a new British fascist party – the National Front – was born in early 1967. The next year Enoch Powell, Conservative MP for Wolverhampton South West, made his “Rivers of Blood” speech. He posed as a brave visionary; perhaps he even believed that he was giving voice to the displaced white community of the Midlands who felt crowded out by Black and Asian immigrants.

I knew straight away what Powell wanted to achieve with the speech: to fan the flames of public dissent. His Oxford education, classical training and powers of oratory served him well. He saw the race card as the way to obtain power. It still is.

Today, a nasty little turd is floating about in our polluted waters. It has many names; one sticks out more than the others. A public schoolboy, posing as “one of the lads”; someone who thought it was funny to hiss at Jewish boys just after the second world war; someone who was given £5m to keep himself safe; someone who got German citizenship legally for his sons (his ex-wife is German) so Brexit disadvantages don’t inconvenience those close to him. There is a widespread fear that Farage (AKA the Odious Niggle) could succeed to the leadership; the kingdom is teetering on the brink of annihilation. But it’s not too late. After all, it is not the lie that passeth through the mind but the lie that sinketh in and settleth in it that doth the hurt. (Thanks, Francis Bacon.) While the bad guys seem to be winning everywhere, I’m not giving up – and neither should you.

Exhausted by but addicted to doomscrolling, sliding from one terrifying headline to another, it’s easy to forget we are all in the same unsteady boat, north or south, young or old, lower, middle and even upper class, ignoring the culprits hiding in plain sight. It’s not the foreigners, legal or illegal, who are pissing on us; it’s the billionaires who own the media and the internet and can pay the debts of the political parties they want to control, and fuck the rest of us. Well, I’m not putting up with it any longer. And neither need you. Let’s have a laugh. It’s the antidote (and all the ammunition) we need to those arseholes who forget that Britain was great before they were born – we can see right through them.

Never forget that laughter is a good medicine, ridicule and satire can change minds, and there’s always sex. Mind you, it’s a while since I enjoyed the full-throated variety, but I know it’s out there.

I refuse to be cut off from the wealth of possibilities that Britain and Ireland offer. Let’s live, have fun, learn new tastes, new words, new mastications. Build bridges, cross chasms. And before we go to the moon again, let’s reap the benefits strangers in our midst offer. It’s not their fault that things are tough. It’s ours. This is my middle finger to naysayers, Nigel Farage and everyone who says “whatever”. It’s time to be Great Britain again – or at least Better Britain. Steady the Buffs and onwards!

This is an edited extract from Miriam’s Full English by Miriam Margolyes, published by John Murray on 3 September at £25. To support the Guardian, order your copy from guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘So many people say things about my appearance – it’s not normal’: Jorja Smith on burnout, body-shaming and finding freedom
EntertainmentTab.text:
It is a sticky, sweltering July afternoon, and I have accidentally found myself at a wake with Jorja Smith. I’m told that the pub where we have met, in the leafiest part of leafy south-west London, is usually a safe bet for an inconspicuous table. But today, sweaty black suits carrying pints drift between tables, and long queues snake round the bar.

Dressed in a simple tank top, bare-faced with her hair scraped back, Smith is waiting for me when I arrive. “I’ve been waiting for my drink for ages,” she says. “But I feel bad saying anything because, you know …”

The sombre mood doesn’t last long – in large part because Smith is effortlessly funny. When her alcohol-free sparkling wine finally arrives, she takes one sip, pauses for the waitress to disappear, then winces theatrically. “Oh,” she says. “That’s not good.” Every time we dissolve into laughter, I glance around guiltily, like we’re schoolgirls trying not to get caught talking at the back of assembly.

It’s hard to imagine a less appropriate setting in which to discuss an album made for sunburnt block parties and 2am raves. What Are the Odds, the 29-year-old’s third album, released this week, is a certified, old-fashioned ass-shaker. Made with Richard Isong – the London producer better known as P2J, whose credits include Beyoncé, Burna Boy and Tems – and featuring the likes of Wizkid and Devlin, it is a vibrant collage of Black British dance music, weaving together UK garage, funky house, 2-step and Afrobeats, into a 12-track collection that pulsates from top to bottom.

While dance music has always been threaded through Smith’s catalogue, usually in the form of a summer single – On My Mind in 2017, Little Things in 2023 – she is better known for her introspective, soulful R&B, as epitomised by her 2016 breakout single Blue Lights (which NME praised as “a fantastically introspective and clever piece of songwriting”, and had critics declaring her Amy Winehouse’s successor). This is the first time she has committed fully to the dancefloor.

“I just love dancing,” Smith shrugs. “I like going out to listen to music, a lot of my friends are DJs. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m outside.”

The genesis of this album was different to her previous records. Her Mercury prize-nominated debut album, Lost & Found, emerged because she felt it was time to make an album. Its successor, Falling Or Flying, arrived because she felt she “needed” a second one. What Are the Odds was made almost accidentally, which is perhaps why it feels so light on its feet.

After making the effervescent club single Little Things with P2J, the pair initially planned to write a dance EP. But the songs kept coming, and the project outgrew itself. “We went through nine songs in the first two days,” Smith says, her eyes widening again at the memory. “I turned up to the studio and he’d made all this music from our conversations. I left and went straight to my label and said: ‘I think this is an album, not an EP. This is serious.’ I’m so excited about it.”

The album may be created for the dancefloor, but its emotional resonance remains unmistakably Smith. For Life mourns losing a friend to addiction; Young Heart is a love letter to Smith’s younger self; The Way It Was meditates on the end of a friendship. “If you just sang the songs with keys or piano,” she says, “they’d all probably be quite sad.”

It is tempting to read What Are the Odds as a comeback album. In the weeks before its release, various headlines have announced Smith’s “return”. When I begin to ask her about this supposed break, she cuts in incredulously. “People keep saying, ‘Oh, you’re back!’ What do you mean, back? I’ve been on tour since 2017. When people say that, I’m like … [you should] check my calendar! People are likely talking about a ‘comeback’,” she says, “because I’m back on social media. I take breaks, and I’m not always out at events and things.”

It’s an astute observation, and one that cuts to the heart of Smith’s unconventional relationship with celebrity. Since Blue Lights announced her arrival as an 18-year-old in 2016, she has become one of British music’s defining voices: a Mercury and Grammy nominee, double Brit award winner, and a featured artist capable of surfacing everywhere from Drake’s More Life to Burna Boy’s African Giant. Yet, she has never cultivated the kind of omnipresent celebrity that feels almost compulsory in the social media age, where visibility seems synonymous with existence. There are no carefully choreographed glimpses into her morning routine, no sense that her life exists to be consumed. Smith has clearly never been especially interested in that side of the bargain.

“I never wanted to be famous,” she says. “I’ve always been quite private. I just wanted to put music out as a teenager and see what happened. I feel really lucky that I’ve got such an amazing fanbase and people really show me love, but fame was never the goal.”

The tension, of course, is that success increasingly lives or dies by the algorithm. The defining British stars of recent years – PinkPantheress, Raye, Lola Young – have all been, in some part, forged in the fires of TikTok. Does Smith ever feel pressure to play that game? “Yeah definitely,” she says. “But, luckily, I’ve got a sick team, and we come up with ideas that we can do that are still me. I don’t want to be here doing trends – you’re not going to catch me doing TikTok dances or any of that stuff.”

Her inclination to privacy also stems from growing up under an unusually unforgiving spotlight. Smith first found an audience by uploading covers to YouTube, recorded from her bedroom in Walsall. Aged 15, she signed with a manager, and began making regular trips to London for songwriting sessions. After finishing her A-levels, she moved to the capital full-time, working shifts in a cafe while trying to carve out a career in music.

Blue Lights, which hauntingly paired Smith’s mellifluous voice with lyrics about police profiling and urban anxiety, landed on SoundCloud in 2016, instantly establishing her as one of the most compelling new voices in British music. The following year, Drake invited her on to his blockbuster playlist, More Life, exposing her to millions of listeners around the world.

Alongside the acclaim, though, came another kind of attention. Almost overnight, Smith became a symbol of a modern beauty ideal, often uncomfortably sexualised before she had properly entered adulthood. For years, the conversation around Jorja Smith the musician existed alongside another conversation entirely, one that Smith had no control over: that of Jorja Smith the face, Jorja Smith the body. “It’s not normal,” she says, reflecting on that time. “Growing up and having so many people having something to say about your appearance.”

The internet, as it tends to do, eventually turned. In the run-up to the release of Falling Or Flying in 2023, every online photo or video seemed to invite commentary on her weight. At one point, the phrase “Jorja Smith weight gain” trended on X for two days. It is something she brings up without prompting.

“It was difficult. I’d be reading things like: ‘What happened to her?’ Or, ‘She’s let herself go.’” She trails off. “It really knocks your confidence.”

On one occasion, she couldn’t resist replying. “Some blog page”– she waves away the name – “had put two photos side by side, like a before and after. I just commented: ‘What the hell, guys? I’m literally 18 in that picture. Why are you doing that?’” She shrugs. “People are so quick. They love you, then they hate you.”

What made that period particularly disorientating, she says, was that the public narrative bore almost no resemblance to reality; at the very moment strangers were dissecting her body online, she felt healthier than ever.

“I’d actually started eating properly,” she says. “Before that, I’d be so busy I’d skip meals, wake up late, I was running every day, obsessively. It was the first time I actually felt healthy, and then people wanted to criticise me? It was a proper headfuck because I was thinking: Wait … can I do anything right?”

For a while, she stopped wanting to do photoshoots, or even go outside for fear of being photographed. “I sort of went into myself,” she says. “I felt like no one could really understand what I was going through.” Her coping mechanisms, she says, are to go for a walk or to the gym, though she catches herself revealing how fragile that equilibrium can still be.

Sometimes she’ll still “see comments … and start thinking: Maybe they’re right?” She stops herself mid-thought. “Oh my God,” she says, laughing in disbelief. “Even me saying that now is crazy. Because they’re just random people!

“But I have my days,” she continues. “I was talking to my mum about it the other day, and she was like: ‘At least they’re not saying you sound shit!’”

One of the ways she’s protected herself is by stepping away from those online platforms. She no longer runs her own social media – her team posts on Instagram, and she only keeps the app to message artists and friends. She hasn’t been on X in years, and never goes looking for commentary about herself.

Part of that self-reclamation meant physically removing herself, too. In 2023, after years in London, she moved back to Walsall – an unusual move for an artist at the height of their career. “I just needed a reset,” she says. “I thought: Let me move back home, touch some grass, see some trees.” London, she says, had become tangled up with the pressures of her career. This City, one of the tracks on What Are the Odds, explores her love-hate relationship with the capital. “Anything negative that happened, I kind of put London as the culprit,” she says. “I was like: ‘I hate this place. I need to get out.’” Distance has since softened London’s hard edges, and today, she divides her time between the West Midlands and the capital: “I’m feeling the buzz of what this place has to offer again, instead of feeling as if I have to wear armour all the time.”

She is fiercely protective, too, of the place she comes from. In an industry so often centred on London, she is keen to keep reminding people that remarkable artists also emerge from elsewhere. “People forget I’m not from London,” she laughs. “And I’m not from Birmingham, either!” In September, Smith will return to Walsall for a home town show at Walsall Arena, a school turned community arts space she used to visit as a girl. Part of Spotify’s Hometown Billboard campaign, the bill doubles as a showcase of local talent: childhood friend Wesley Joseph, with whom she released the single July this year, supports, alongside the Blue Lights Choir she founded to create opportunities for young people in the town. “I hope it’s a moment that inspires the next generation to believe that big things really can come from Walsall,” she says.

These days, when she isn’t working, she is trying to build a life that exists beyond music. She walks, cooks and has rediscovered running. “I’ve signed up for the London marathon next year,” she says. “I wanted a goal, and I watched everyone finishing it this year and thought: That’s such a sick thing to do.”

Despite her instinct to retreat from the spotlight, Smith is also consciously trying to step back into the world. Recently, she was on the phone with a friend back home when she mentioned turning down an invitation to a Vogue party. Her friend wouldn’t let it slide. “She was like, ‘Go! Not everyone gets invited to these things. You only live once. If you keep turning everything down, you’re going to be 70 and have zero stories of fun nights out because you never went anywhere!’” she laughs.

Outside, the heat hasn’t lifted. Mourners are still in the beer garden. As she gets up to leave, Smith pulls a cap low over her face and slides on a pair of oversized sunglasses. Until that moment, it has been surprisingly easy to forget that she is famous at all.

“It’s all about finding that balance,” she says, smiling as she stands. “But I’m feeling good. I’m starting to feel like my younger self again.”

What Are the Odds is out now on FAMM. Jorja Smith performs at Walsall Arena on 6 September.
